Chaetostoma leucomelas Eigenmann, 1918. Common name: Magdalena Tiger Chaetostoma. Synonym: Chaetostomus leucomelas. Size: 143 mm (5.6") SL.

Etymology: Greek, chaite = hair + Greek, stoma = mouth. The specific epithet refers to its white (leukos = white) and black (melas = black) colouring.

Type locality: Río Patía, halfway between the Río Magui and Río Telembi, Colombia.

IUCN Red List: Least Concern (last assessed 2014).
South America: Patía and upper Cauca River basins in Colombia (Colombian Pacific rivers: Patía; Colombian Caribbean rivers: Magdalena, Cauca).
Well rounded stones stacked to replicate a river bottom and provide caves.

Males have a larger and broader head, slimmer ventral sides and disproportionately large pelvic fins. The over-sized pelvic fins perhaps play a large role in fertilization of the eggs: by inverting them over the clutch, the males prevent the sperm cells being carried away by fast water current.

Identification: The genus Chaetostoma is not straightforward to identify, but as a general rule, the species has spines behind the gill-cover (interopercular odontodes), no plates on the abdomen, and aside from C. platyrhynchus also lacks plates on the snout edge. It differs from Ancistrus by not having fleshy tentacles on the snout.
Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society v. 56 (no. 7), pp 681.
